title: Ducks and geese

identification.basis: The dictionary has nili-nili 'duck' and jamarbina 'goose'. The Atlas records the Pacific black duck, hardhead, grey teal, green and cotton pygmy geese, plumed whistling duck, wood duck, pink-eared duck, radjah shelduck and magpie goose within 30 km of Karma Waters.

summary: **[nili-nili](word:nili-nili)** is a duck and **[jamarbina](word:jamarbina)** a goose, and the dictionary stops there, which leaves the ten kinds on the Karma Waters lagoons to sort out by eye [ref:hershberger1982]. The Pacific black duck, thirty records within 30 km, is the duck of every pool; the hardhead dives, the grey teal dabbles, the green pygmy goose sits among the lily pads, the plumed whistling ducks stand in whistling mobs on the bank, the wood ducks graze the grass like small geese, the pink-eared duck strains the plankton of the drying pans with its spoon bill, the radjah shelduck works the paperbark swamps, and the magpie goose, the big black-and-white goose of the floodplain, comes through in the dry [ref:ala-aves] [ref:wiki-pbd] [ref:wiki-hardhead] [ref:wiki-green-pygmy-goose] [ref:wiki-plumed-wd] [ref:wiki-wood-duck] [ref:wiki-pink-eared-duck] [ref:wiki-radjah] [ref:wiki-magpie-goose]. Roth's ducks were 'stalked and speared', the hunter gliding through the water with a collar of grass round his head 'like a tussock of grass floating down the stream', or knocked over 'with long thin switches ... both by day and by moonlight', or noosed from a feather-quill on a stick, or, near the Laura and at Cape Bedford, 'caught by silently diving under them in the water and pulling them down' [ref:roth1901]. The eggs were taken in the nesting season, which here is the wet, in hollows and on the ground [ref:roth1901] [ref:wiki-pbd].

infobox.label: Food
infobox.value: Seeds, weed, lily seed, insects, shrimps and snails; the hardhead dives, the pink-eared strains, the wood duck grazes, the magpie goose digs

infobox.label: Breeding
infobox.value: Mostly the wet; nests in tree hollows (black duck, pygmy geese, wood duck, shelduck), on the ground or in reeds

infobox.label: Taken by
infobox.value: Stalked and speared under a grass hood; knocked down with switches by day or moonlight; noosed; dived under and pulled down

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[nili-nili](word:nili-nili)** 'duck'; **[jamarbina](word:jamarbina)** 'goose' [ref:hershberger1982]. The dictionary's speakers were coastal and rainforest people, and the duck words are few; the Western Yalanji of the Mitchell lagoons may well have more, and the contribution box on this page is for them. The birds of the same water with their own words: **[dulku](word:dulku)** 'white crane', **[biluwarra](word:biluwarra)** 'spoon bill bird', **[birmba](word:birmba)** 'straw-necked ibis', **[kalmbangarr](word:kalmbangarr)** 'black diver bird', **[kulbal](word:kulbal)** 'brolga', on the [water birds](entry:water-birds) and [cranes](entry:brolga-and-cranes) pages [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: The ducks and geese of the upper Mitchell
sections.body:
**Pacific black duck** (*Anas superciliosa*), thirty records. 'A dark body, and a paler head with a dark crown and facial stripes. In flight, it shows a green speculum and pale underwing ... The size range is 54–61 cm'. 'This sociable duck is found in a variety of wetland habitats ... It feeds by upending'. 'The nest is usually placed in a hole in a tree, but sometimes an old nest of a corvid is used and occasionally the nest will be placed on the ground. The clutch of 8–10 pale cream eggs is incubated only by the female. The eggs hatch after 26–32 days' [ref:wiki-pbd].

**Hardhead** (*Aythya australis*), twenty-six records. 'Smaller than most ducks, with body length typically between 42–59 cm', 'a fairly uniform chocolate-brown above, with rufous flanks and white undersides'; the male has a white eye. 'Hardheads feed by diving deeply, often staying submerged for as long as a minute at a time. They slip under the water with barely a ripple ... They eat a broad range of small aquatic creatures, and supplement this with water weeds.' 'Moderately nomadic in normal years, but disperse widely in times of drought' [ref:wiki-hardhead].

**Grey teal** (*Anas gracilis*), fifteen records, 'a dabbling duck found in open wetlands', small and mottled grey-brown with a pale throat; it 'nests near its favoured freshwater lakes and marshes, usually on the ground, but also in tree holes' [ref:wiki-grey-teal].

**Green pygmy goose** (*Nettapus pulchellus*), twenty-two records. 'Ranging from 30 to 36 cm in length, the green pygmy goose is one of the smallest species of duck ... The breeding male has a predominantly dark green back and neck, and a dark gray crown. The cheeks are white, and the underparts are pale grey and white scalloped'; 'the green pygmy goose nests in tree hollows. Eight to twelve eggs are laid and the incubation period is 26 days'. It lives on the lily lagoons [ref:wiki-green-pygmy-goose]. The **cotton pygmy goose** (*N. coromandelianus*), five records, is smaller still, 'the smallest waterfowl on earth, at as little as 160 g and 26 cm', white-faced, feeding 'mainly at the surface of the water' [ref:wiki-cotton-pygmy-goose].

**Plumed whistling duck** (*Dendrocygna eytoni*), eight records, 'also called the grass whistling duck'. 'Measuring 42–60 cm and weighing around one kilogram, it is a long-necked duck with brown upperparts, paler underparts and a white rump. The chest is a chestnut colour with thin black bars, while long black-margined plumes arise from its flanks. Its bill and legs are a pinkish red'; 'the call is a characteristic whistle'. The wandering whistling duck, two records, is its darker relative that swims more [ref:wiki-plumed-wd] [ref:ala-aves].

**Wood duck** (*Chenonetta jubata*), eight records. 'This 45–51 cm duck looks like a small goose, and mostly feeds by grazing in flocks. The male is grey with a dark brown head, mottled breast ... The female has white stripes above and below the eye'; it nests in hollows [ref:wiki-wood-duck].

**Pink-eared duck** (*Malacorhynchus membranaceus*), six records. 'A large spatulate bill ... Its brown back and crown, black and white barred sides and black eye patches on its otherwise white face make this bird unmistakable'. 'They are dependent on plankton, as well as crustaceans, mollusks and insects. Their bill is well designed for straining minute organisms'; 'nesting is stimulated by the drying and filling of pools' [ref:wiki-pink-eared-duck].

**Radjah shelduck** (*Radjah radjah*), four records. 'Both the male and female of the species are mostly white, with dark wing-tips and a distinctive "collar" of dark feathers'; 'the species prefers the salty waters of mangrove flats and paperbark tree swamps, but will visit all manner of brackish and freshwater swamps, lagoons, lakes'; it eats 'mollusks, aquatic or other insects, worms, aquatic weeds' and nests 'often in the hollow limb' of a tree [ref:wiki-radjah].

**Magpie goose** (*Anseranas semipalmata*), three records, the goose of the north. 'Black-and-white plumage in both sexes, with a long neck and legs and a long hooked bill. The males are 75–90 cm in length and weigh 2.76 kg on average ... Their voice is a loud resonant honking.' 'Found in a variety of open wetland areas such as floodplains and swamps, where they wade and swim. They eat mostly vegetation such as dry grass blades, grass seeds, spike rush bulbs and wild rice'. 'Colonial breeders ... gregarious outside of the breeding season when they can form large and noisy flocks of up to a few thousand individuals. Magpie geese nest on the ground or in trees'. In western Arnhem Land 'it became an important food item with the formation of wetlands about 1500 years ago, and is depicted in rock art from this period' [ref:wiki-magpie-goose].

**Roth's methods, 1901.** 'The natives of the upper Georgina and in the Boulia District noose ducks with a long slender stick, to the extremity of which a feather-quill with slip-noose is attached. The hunter, well concealed with bushes tied round his head and face, waits patiently in the water for his prey, which, paddling along the water, soon comes into suitable position for the loop to be slipped over its neck.' 'In the hinterland of Princess Charlotte Bay, on the Palmer River, etc., ducks, geese, and similar game are all stalked and speared, usually with the ordinary simple-point spear if on land, but commonly with a pronged one if on water. In either case, the aboriginal covers his head with a bundle of long grass, tied about near to its extremities into something like a horse-collar, the ends falling over onto the back of the wearer's shoulders ... holding with one hand a bunch of leafy switches in front, and with the other his wommera spear, as he glides forward in the water after the unsuspecting birds. Viewed from the front, the individual so concealed looks for all the world like a tussock of grass floating down the stream, so slow and silent are all his movements. If duck are being hunted out on the plains, the black does not trouble about holding the leafy screen in front of him, but stalks his prey more or less on all fours, under cover of any intervening bushes. On the Pennefather, Embley, Tully, etc., Rivers, ducks and geese may be knocked over with long thin switches both by day and by moonlight. The Pennefather natives, in addition, will build special bush-shelters in the lagoons, and hiding under cover will wait there for hours for a favourable strike with their spears. In the neighbourhood of the Laura, also at Cape Bedford and elsewhere, ducks can be caught by silently diving under them in the water and pulling them down' [ref:roth1901]. Murrell, near Bowen, saw birds caught 'with snares, merely loose knots, which are placed in the thick grass and reeds in the swamps, and as the birds pass through in quest of food, especially at night time, the prey is caught' [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Telling the ducks
sections.body:
- **Black duck**: dark, with two black stripes on a pale face; upends; the common one [ref:wiki-pbd].
- **Hardhead**: chocolate brown, a white eye on the male, slips under and stays down; never upends [ref:wiki-hardhead].
- **Grey teal**: small, pale-throated, in mobs on open water [ref:wiki-grey-teal].
- **Pygmy geese**: tiny, green-backed or white-faced, perched on the lily pads [ref:wiki-green-pygmy-goose] [ref:wiki-cotton-pygmy-goose].
- **Plumed whistling duck**: upright, long-necked, with plumes along the flanks, in whistling crowds on the bank by day [ref:wiki-plumed-wd].
- **Wood duck**: a small grey goose grazing on the grass, the male with a dark mane [ref:wiki-wood-duck].
- **Pink-eared duck**: zebra sides, a black eye patch, a spoon of a bill [ref:wiki-pink-eared-duck].
- **Radjah shelduck**: white with a dark collar, in the paperbarks [ref:wiki-radjah].
- **Magpie goose**: big, black and white, a knob on the head, honking, half-webbed feet that perch in trees [ref:wiki-magpie-goose].
- **[Cormorants and the darter](entry:water-birds)** sit low and dive; they are not ducks [ref:wiki-darter].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Whistling** from the bank: plumed whistling ducks [ref:wiki-plumed-wd].
- **Honking** overhead in lines in the dry: magpie geese on the move [ref:wiki-magpie-goose].
- **A duck gone under without a ripple** and up a minute later: a hardhead [ref:wiki-hardhead].
- **Down and eggshell at a hollow** above the water in the wet [ref:wiki-pbd].
- **Grazed grass by the pool** in the morning: wood ducks [ref:wiki-wood-duck].
- **Birds strung along a drying pan** with their bills in the scum: pink-eared ducks [ref:wiki-pink-eared-duck].

sections.heading: Where they are
sections.body: The long pools of the Mitchell and the lagoons and swamps off it; the lily lagoons for the pygmy geese; the paperbark swamps for the shelduck; the drying pans for the pink-eared duck; the grass by the water for the wood duck and the whistlers; the floodplain for the magpie goose [ref:wiki-green-pygmy-goose] [ref:wiki-radjah] [ref:wiki-pink-eared-duck] [ref:wiki-wood-duck] [ref:wiki-magpie-goose]. The [waterhole](entry:waterhole) page has the pools' year, and the station's river camps are beside them [ref:kw-camping].

sections.heading: The duck's lagoon
sections.body: The ducks eat the seed of the grass and the sedges, the weed, the lily seed, the insects and shrimps of the shallows, each in its own way, dabbling, diving, grazing, straining; the magpie goose digs the spike-rush bulbs and the [cranes](entry:brolga-and-cranes) dig beside it [ref:wiki-pbd] [ref:wiki-hardhead] [ref:wiki-pink-eared-duck] [ref:wiki-magpie-goose] [ref:wiki-brolga]. They are hunted by the [sea eagle and the kites](entry:woodland), by the [freshwater crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile), by the [goanna](entry:goanna) at the nest, and by people [ref:wiki-wedgie] [ref:roth1901]. Their nesting hollows are the same old [bloodwoods](entry:bloodwood) and paperbarks that the [possums](entry:possums) and parrots use, which is one more reason to leave the hollow trees standing [ref:wiki-pbd] [ref:re-woodland].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Nesting with the rains, in hollows and reeds, eggs 'in the nesting season' being Roth's season for taking them; the ducks concentrate on the shrinking pools through the dry, and the pink-eared ducks and magpie geese come and go with the filling and drying of the pans [ref:roth1901] [ref:wiki-pink-eared-duck] [ref:wiki-magpie-goose]. The late dry, when every duck on the river is on the last pools, is the easy time for the hunter and the hard time for the duck [ref:griffith2021]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Meat**: speared under a grass hood, knocked down with switches, noosed, dived under and pulled down [ref:roth1901].
- **Eggs** in the nesting season [ref:roth1901].
- **Down and feathers** for the camp's ornaments [ref:anderson1996].
- **A sign of water**: whistling ducks and geese overhead in the dry are going to water.

sections.heading: Taking ducks the old way
sections.body:
From Roth [ref:roth1901]:

1. **The grass hood**: tie a bundle of long grass round the head like a horse-collar, the ends over the shoulders; in the water, hold leafy switches in front with one hand and the woomera spear in the other, and move so slowly that you are a floating tussock [ref:roth1901].
2. **Use the pronged spear** on the water, the plain point on land; on the plain, crawl under bushes [ref:roth1901].
3. **By moonlight**, ducks roosting on the bank can be knocked over with long thin switches [ref:roth1901].
4. **The noose**: a feather-quill slip-noose on a long slender stick, slipped over the neck of a duck paddling past the hidden hunter [ref:roth1901].
5. **The dive**: swim under a sitting duck and pull it down by the legs, the Laura and Cape Bedford way [ref:roth1901].
6. **A hide in the lagoon**: a bush shelter in the water, and hours of waiting [ref:roth1901].
7. **Cook** on the coals or in the [earth oven](entry:earth-oven); pluck first [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Native birds are protected wildlife in Queensland under the *Nature Conservation Act 1992*; native title holders hunting for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs are covered by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993*, recognised in the Western Yalanji determinations [ref:qld-nca] [ref:alrc] [ref:wyac2020]. The wood duck is a declared game bird in some states but not in Queensland, where no recreational duck season exists [ref:wiki-wood-duck] [ref:qld-nca].
- Wading a lagoon under a grass hood is wading a crocodile's lagoon; the old method belongs to pools you know, in daylight, with a watcher [ref:crocwise].
- Lead shot is banned for waterfowl across Australia; the old methods never had the problem.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Ten kinds of duck and goose use the Karma Waters pools, and the black duck, hardhead and green pygmy goose are on them most days of the dry [ref:ala-aves]. The dictionary's two words are a start; the Western Yalanji names for the whistler, the diver and the big goose are for the contribution box below [ref:hershberger1982].
